content.text: {"persuasion":"PERSUADED","support_scope":"FULL","rationale":"The book's definition — cleansing removes the defilement that bars proper contact, approach, or use; clean means free of that defilement and fit for its permitted place; uncleanness may be physical, ceremonial, or moral and is not identical with guilt — explains every printed text without strain. The common interpretation, which treats unclean as essentially a symbol of sin and cleansing as essentially forgiveness/sanctification, must either impute guilt where Scripture assigns none (Lev 12:2 childbirth, Lev 15:18 marital relations, Num 19:11 corpse contact — the last two being commanded or obligatory acts) or add an unsupported typological layer ('symbolizes sin without being sin') that the texts themselves never state. The book, by contrast, absorbs the moral uses (Ps 51:2,10; 1 John 1:7,9) without contradiction, because sin genuinely defiles and thus falls inside the removal-of-defilement definition. The book also preserves a distinction the texts explicitly draw and the common reading blurs: Lev 10:10 keeps holy/common and clean/unclean as two separate lines, and Eph 5:26 keeps 'sanctify' and 'cleanse' as two operations, which the book's paired definitions explain and the collapsed sin-purity reading treats as redundancy. On inference to best explanation across the supplied evidence, the book wins.","book_core_identification":"To cleanse is to remove defilement that bars proper contact, approach, or use; 'clean' is what is free of that defilement and fit for its permitted place. Uncleanness is a fitness-status that may be physical, ceremonial, or moral; it does not always entail sin or guilt (childbirth, marital relations, corpse contact defile without transgression), though sin does defile, so the vocabulary carries moral weight in passages like Psalm 51 and 1 John 1 without changing its shape.","book_secondary_elaborations":["Cleansing is distinct from sanctification: cleansing removes what makes a vessel unfit, while sanctification places the cleansed vessel under a holy owner's claim and appointed use (Eph 5:26; 2 Tim 2:21; 1 Cor 6:11).","The opposite of clean is unclean, while the opposite of holy is common/profane — two separate lines the priests were charged to keep distinct (Lev 10:10; Ezek 22:26).","The method claim that definitions must survive every use of the word across the canon rather than being built from a favored doctrinal passage."],"strongest_counter_interpretation":"The mainstream Christian reading: clean/unclean is ritual-purity language whose real referent is moral and spiritual condition before God — uncleanness symbolizes sin, defilement, and unfitness for God's holy presence, and cleansing symbolizes forgiveness and sanctification accomplished through Christ's atoning blood, with the Levitical washings read as types of that spiritual cleansing (Ps 51; Isa 1:16-18; Ezek 36:25; Mark 7; Heb 9-10; 1 John 1:7,9).","counter_core_identification":"Unclean essentially signifies sin and moral defilement before God; to cleanse essentially signifies God's forgiveness and sanctification of the sinner, with the Old Testament ritual system functioning as typology of that spiritual reality rather than as a distinct fitness-status category in its own right.","counter_relation_to_book_core":"CONTRADICTS","material_core_denial":"The counter denies that uncleanness is fundamentally a non-culpable fitness-status; it identifies uncleanness with sin-defilement (at least symbolically) as the word's primary meaning, whereas the book asserts that uncleanness and guilt are not identical and that many defilements carry no transgression at all.","counter_case":["The prophets and psalms explicitly moralize the vocabulary: 'Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin' (Ps 51:2) and 'Create in me a clean heart' (Ps 51:10) make cleansing a matter of forgiveness and inner renewal.","1 John 1:7,9 ties cleansing directly to the blood of Christ and forgiveness of sins, and Eph 5:26 to Christ's sanctifying work on the church — the New Testament's dominant use is moral-spiritual.","Hebrews 9-10 reads the Levitical purifications as shadows whose reality is the cleansing of the conscience by Christ's blood, licensing a typological reading in which ritual impurity always pointed to sin.","Jesus relocates defilement from external ritual to the heart (Mark 7:14-23), suggesting the ritual categories were always provisional symbols of moral defilement.","This reading matches the broad devotional and homiletical consensus of Christian teaching."],"book_explanatory_advantages":["Explains the non-culpable defilements printed with the entry without contradiction: Lev 12:2 (childbirth), Lev 15:18 (marital relations, within a commanded institution), and Num 19:11 (corpse contact, an unavoidable duty) all produce uncleanness with no sin named; the counter must either impute guilt the text never assigns or add an unstated symbolic layer.","Explains why Lev 10:10 lists two distinct oppositions — holy/unholy and unclean/clean — rather than one; the book's two-line framework (fitness vs. ownership-status) accounts for the double pairing, which the sin-symbolism reading collapses.","Explains Eph 5:26 and 1 Cor 6:11 without redundancy: 'sanctify and cleanse' / 'washed, sanctified, justified' are three distinct operations answering three distinct questions, not synonyms for 'made spiritually better'.","Fully absorbs the moral uses (Ps 51:2,10; 1 John 1:7,9; Isa 1:16-18) because sin genuinely defiles, so moral cleansing is a species of the book's definition rather than counter-evidence to it.","Coheres with the accepted prior findings on this provider — righteousness as right-living, justification as verdict, works as deeds-as-such — in which the book consistently distinguishes status-lines Scripture keeps separate rather than merging them into one soteriological abstraction."],"counter_explanatory_advantages":["Better captures the New Testament's typological trajectory (Heb 9-10; Mark 7) in which the ritual system is explicitly read as shadow pointing to conscience-cleansing through Christ.","Matches the felt weight of the vocabulary in devotional use, where cleansing overwhelmingly means forgiveness of sin.","Simpler as a homiletical summary: one meaning (purity from sin) rather than a graded category with physical, ceremonial, and moral registers."],"evidence_book_core_cannot_explain":[],"comparative_winner":"BOOK","decisive_sources":["Leviticus 12:2 — childbirth makes a woman unclean seven days with no sin named; the counter's identification of uncleanness with sin cannot explain this without an unsupported added step, while the book's fitness-status definition explains it directly.","Leviticus 15:18 — marital relations, commanded and blessed elsewhere, produce uncleanness until evening; guilt-symbolism strains here, fitness-status does not.","Numbers 19:11 — touching the dead, an obligatory duty (burial), defiles for seven days; uncleanness as a bar on approach, not a verdict of wickedness.","Leviticus 10:10 with Ezekiel 22:26 — Scripture itself keeps holy/common and clean/unclean as two separate distinctions, which the book's framework preserves and the counter collapses.","Ephesians 5:26 and 1 Corinthians 6:11 — 'sanctify and cleanse' and 'washed, sanctified, justified' are distinct operations, confirming that cleansing (removing defilement) is not simply a synonym for sanctification or forgiveness.","Psalm 51:2,10 and 1 John 1:7,9 — the moral uses, which the book explains as sin-defilement falling within its broader definition, showing the book's core loses none of the counter's genuine evidence."],"unresolved_objections":["The entry does not itself address the New Testament typological texts (Mark 7:14-23; Acts 10; Heb 9-10) that the common interpretation leans on; the book's framework can accommodate them (moral defilement is real defilement; the shadow/reality contrast concerns which cleansing avails), but the printed proving chapter does not work them out explicitly.","Whether ritual impurity, though non-culpable, was nonetheless divinely designed as typology of sin and death (the Milgrom/Wenham death-symbolism layer) is left open; the book defines the word's function without ruling on the system's symbolic rationale.","The precise boundary between 'clean' and 'fit for permitted place' in fully moral contexts (e.g., 1 John 1:9's 'cleanse us from all unrighteousness') is asserted rather than exhaustively demonstrated from every occurrence."],"confidence":"high"}
